languedeboeuf.resume: A surprising blood-red bracket on old oaks and sweet chestnuts.
identification: Bracket red like a tongue or a liver, moist
Marbled red flesh that oozes red juice
Cream underside with small separate tubes
usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

chanterelletube.resume: A small brown chanterelle with a yellow stem, in troops among the moss of conifer forests.
identification: Brown funnel-shaped cap, often pierced in the centre
Underside with grey-yellow ridges (no true gills)
Hollow yellow stem
usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

russulecharbon.resume: One of the most common brittlegills under broadleaf trees.
identification: Violet to greenish, multicoloured cap
Supple white gills, greasy to the touch (they don't break)
White flesh that breaks like chalk

sosies.diff: Several brittlegills are poisonous, and a green death cap can get mixed in. Have each specimen checked.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

rougissante.resume: Edible when well cooked, but it's an Amanita: confusing it with the panther cap is far too easy.
identification: Pinkish-brown cap with grey-beige flakes
Flesh that slowly turns RED where damaged or nibbled by slugs
Striated ring

sosies.diff: Pure white flakes, flesh that doesn't redden, smooth ring. Seriously poisonous.

usages: Not advised for anyone except experienced mycologists.
Poisonous raw.

printaniere.resume: An entirely white deadly Amanita… in spring, when you don't expect it.
identification: All white, smooth cap
White gills, ring, sac-like volva at the base

sosies.diff: No ring or volva, smell of flour. Always dig out the base of the stem.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

lepiote.resume: A small Lepiota of parks and edges, with the same toxins as the death cap.
identification: Small cap 2 to 5 cm, concentric pinkish-brown scales
Free white gills
Stem banded with pinkish zones

sosies.diff: Cap over 15 cm, sliding double ring. Rule: no Lepiota under 10 cm.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

gyromitre.resume: The “false morel” of conifer woods. Its toxins also evaporate during cooking.
identification: Red-brown cap folded like a brain
Chambered inside, not hollow

sosies.diff: Cap with regular pits, completely hollow when cut.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

omphalote.resume: Large bright orange clumps at the foot of oaks and olive trees, confused with the chanterelle.
identification: Bright orange clumps on wood or buried stumps
True crowded gills running down the stem

sosies.diff: Thick, forked ridges (no gills), grows singly on the ground, never in a large clump on wood.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

paxille.resume: Long eaten, it can trigger a deadly immune reaction after several meals.
identification: Brown cap with its edge ROLLED inwards
Yellowish gills that turn brown when touched and come off easily
Very common under birch
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

equestre.resume: The “man on horseback”, once prized: repeated meals destroy the muscles.
identification: Greenish-yellow cap, browner centre
Sulphur-yellow gills
Under pines, on sandy soil
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

tigre.resume: A large grey mushroom causing severe digestive poisoning.
identification: Grey cap covered with dark scales in a tiger pattern
Cream-white gills, smell of flour
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

clitoblanc.resume: A small white lawn mushroom, growing among fairy ring champignons.
identification: White to cream cap, as if dusted with frost
Crowded gills running down the stem
usages: Eat nothing. Symptoms: sweating, tears, salivation within the hour: call the poison centre.

noirdencre.resume: Eaten with alcohol (or up to 72 h before or after), it causes hot flushes, palpitations and fainting.
identification: Grey bell-shaped, pleated cap, in clumps
Gills that dissolve into black ink
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

emetique.resume: A bright red brittlegill of damp forests, very acrid, causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
identification: Bright red, smooth, shiny cap
Pure white gills and stem
Brittle, very hot-tasting flesh
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

satan.resume: A large, stocky bolete of chalky soils, with red pores and a whitish cap.
identification: Greyish-white cap
Blood-red pores
Swollen red stem with a net pattern
Flesh that turns blue, unpleasant smell as it ages
usages: Simple rule: reject all boletes with red pores.

psilocybe.resume: A small meadow mushroom, hallucinogenic. Possessing it is illegal, and poisonings regularly end up in A&E.
identification: Small, pointed conical cap, beige to brown
Very thin, wavy stem
In damp grazed meadows
usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

arbousier.resume: The “tree strawberries” of the maquis. When fully ripe, they are sweet and mealy.
identification: Shrub with shiny, finely toothed evergreen leaves
Round, rough fruits, yellow then bright red
White bell-shaped flowers at the same time as the fruit
usages: Only fully red, soft fruits.
In small amounts: overripe, they ferment slightly.

figuebarbarie.resume: A cactus with flat “pads”. Its fruits are delicious but covered in tiny spines that stick everywhere.
identification: Fleshy oval pad-shaped stems
Oval green to red fruits on the edge of the pads
Tufts of tiny spines (glochids) on the fruits
usages: Never touch with bare hands: use tongs or a thick cloth.
Roll the fruits on the ground with a stick, then peel them with a knife.

pinparasol.resume: Its large cones release pine nuts, very nourishing.
identification: Characteristic umbrella-shaped crown
Long needles in pairs
Large, heavy cones containing hard-shelled seeds
usages: Warm the cone near the fire so it opens, then crack the shell of the pine nuts.

thym.resume: A small, very fragrant shrub of the garrigue.
identification: Sub-shrub 10 to 30 cm, woody stems
Tiny rolled grey leaves
Strong characteristic smell when crushed
usages: As a tea or to flavour a dish.
Pick a few sprigs without uprooting the plant.

romarin.resume: An aromatic shrub of the garrigue and coasts.
identification: Shrub with needle-like leaves, dark green above, white below, rolled edges
Pale blue flowers
Camphor-like smell

sosies.diff: Flat needles, plain green on both sides, no smell. Deadly.

usages: As a tea or to flavour grilled meat.

asperge.resume: Thin bitter shoots, much sought after in spring in the maquis.
identification: Spiny bush with prickly needle-like “leaves”
In spring, thin green shoots with tight tips coming from the base

sosies.diff: Climbing shoots with no spiny bush around them, tip that coils. Poisonous, very irritant.

usages: Cook the shoots like asparagus (omelette).

laurierrose.resume: An ornamental shrub found everywhere in the south of France, deadly for the heart. Even the smoke from its wood is dangerous.
identification: Narrow, leathery leaves, grouped in threes
Large pink, white or red flowers in bunches
usages: Eat nothing. Never use it as a skewer for food or burn it.

datura.resume: A weed of fields and waste ground, spreading. Its seeds have already contaminated crops.
identification: Large white trumpet-shaped flowers
Spiny capsule fruit the size of a walnut
Unpleasant smell
usages: Eat nothing.

ricin.resume: Its mottled seeds contain one of the most powerful plant toxins.
identification: Large palmate leaves with 5–11 lobes, often reddish
Spiny capsule fruits containing shiny mottled seeds
usages: Eat nothing.

lactaire.resume: The “saffron” of pine woods: it oozes an orange milk.
identification: Orange cap with concentric rings
Carrot-ORANGE milk where broken, turning green
Under pines

sosies.diff: Hairy cap edge, very acrid WHITE milk. Poisonous.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist before eating.

aspic.resume: The most common viper in France. It likes sunny scree, low walls and edges.
identification: Stocky snake 60 to 75 cm long, slightly upturned snout
Back markings in bars or a broken zigzag
Vertical pupil

sosies.diff: Slimmer, round pupil, large scales on the head. Harmless.

usages: If bitten: stay calm, lie down, keep the limb still, remove rings and watch.
Don't suck, cut or apply a tourniquet. Call 112.

processionpin.resume: Moves in long lines on the ground at the end of winter. Dangerous for dogs and children.
identification: Hairy orange-brown caterpillars following each other in single file
White silky ball-shaped nests at the tips of pine branches
usages: Don't touch the caterpillars or the nests, keep dogs on a lead.
If contact: don't rub, rinse with water, change clothes, see a doctor if the eyes or mouth are affected.

veratre.resume: Grows in the same mountain pastures as great yellow gentian. The confusion is deadly and happens every year.
identification: Large leaves pleated like an accordion, ALTERNATE (one by one, in a spiral) along the stem
Downy underside to the leaves
Clusters of white-green flowers in summer

sosies.diff: Leaves OPPOSITE in pairs, smooth underneath, yellow flowers. Protected in many regions: don't pick.

usages: Eat nothing.

airelle.resume: Small, tart red berries of heaths and mountain forests.
identification: Small shrub with leathery, shiny evergreen leaves, with black dots underneath
Shiny red berries in clusters

sosies.diff: Leaves without black dots underneath, mealy, tasteless berries. Avoid.

usages: Raw (tart) or cooked as a compote.
